title: Angular Momentum of Rigid Bodies and General Planar Decomposition
learning_objective: Determine the angular momentum of rigid bodies undergoing fixed-axis rotation and combined translation-rotation relative to arbitrary reference points.
explanation: For a symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed principal axis of symmetry passing through its center of mass, every particle executes circular motion with $v_i = r_i \omega$. Summing particle angular momenta yields: $$\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}$$ where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the rotation axis. For general planar motion (combined translation and rotation), the angular momentum evaluated with respect to an arbitrary fixed origin $O$ in an inertial frame decomposes into two distinct, decoupled components: $$\vec{L}_O = \vec{L}_{\text{cm}} + \vec{r}_{\text{cm}} \times M \vec{v}_{\text{cm}} = I_{\text{cm}} \vec{\omega} + \vec{r}_{\text{cm}} \times M \vec{v}_{\text{cm}}$$ Here, $\vec{L}_{\text{cm}} = I_{\text{cm}} \vec{\omega}$ is the intrinsic 'spin' angular momentum about the center of mass, while $\vec{r}_{\text{cm}} \times M \vec{v}_{\text{cm}}$ is the 'orbital' angular momentum of a point particle of mass $M$ located at the center of mass moving with velocity $\vec{v}_{\text{cm}}$.
intuition: Total angular momentum about an external point consists of two parts: how the body spins about its own waist ($ec{L}_{\text{spin}} = I_{\text{cm}} \vec{\omega}$), plus how its center of mass sweeps out angle around the external pivot ($ec{L}_{\text{orbital}} = \vec{r}_{\text{cm}} \times \vec{P}$). Just like Earth has spin angular momentum (day-night cycle) and orbital angular momentum (orbiting the Sun).
formal_definition: The angular momentum of an extended body about an origin O in terms of its center of mass motion: $$\vec{L}_O = \sum \vec{r}_i \times m_i \vec{v}_i = I_{\text{cm}} \vec{\omega} + \vec{r}_{\text{cm}} \times M \vec{v}_{\text{cm}}$$
assumptions: Planar motion where angular velocity vector is perpendicular to motion plane
Reference point O is fixed in an inertial reference frame
boundary_conditions: Holds for any rigid body undergoing planar translation and rotation
If rotation axis is not a principal axis of inertia, L vector is not parallel to omega
source_references: Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol 1, Chapter 19
